questions.question: A screen keeps a search query in `var query by remember { mutableStateOf("") }`. The user rotates the device (the Activity is recreated). What happens to the query?
options: It resets to an empty string; `rememberSaveable` (or a ViewModel) is needed to keep it across recreation
It is kept, because `remember` stores its value in the Activity's saved instance state Bundle
It is kept, because a recomposition and an Activity recreation are treated the same way by `remember`
It is kept only on API 34 and higher, where Compose preserves the slot table across rotation
questions.explanation: `remember` only lives as long as the composition, and recreating the Activity builds a new one. `rememberSaveable` writes to the saved-state registry, so it survives configuration changes and process death (for Bundle-able types or with a Saver). A ViewModel survives configuration changes but not process death.

questions.question: `derivedStateOf` is useful when an input state changes more often than the result you care about, for example `showScrollToTop` derived from `listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0`.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The index changes on every scrolled item, but the boolean only flips occasionally; `derivedStateOf` makes readers recompose only when the derived value changes. Using it for a value that changes as often as its input just adds overhead. It is usually wrapped in `remember` so the derived state is not recreated on each recomposition.

questions.question: With strong skipping mode enabled (the default in recent Compose compiler versions), how are a composable's parameters compared to decide whether it can be skipped?
options: Parameters are not compared at all; a composable is skipped whenever its parent recomposes for any reason
Any unstable parameter still makes the composable non-skippable, as it was before strong skipping existed
Every parameter is compared with equals(), whether or not the compiler inferred its type to be stable
Stable parameters are compared with equals(); unstable ones by instance identity (===), so the same instance lets it skip
questions.explanation: Strong skipping makes composables with unstable parameters skippable, using reference equality for those parameters and `equals()` for stable ones; it also auto-remembers lambdas. So passing the same `List` instance skips, while building a new list each recomposition does not. Stability still matters: it decides whether a structurally equal new object counts as 'unchanged'.

questions.question: Why is `Modifier.offset { IntOffset(0, scroll.value) }` preferred over `Modifier.offset(y = scroll.value.dp)` for a value that changes every frame?
options: The lambda form runs on a background thread, so per-frame offset changes cannot block the main thread
The dp version is deprecated and does not trigger any update when the state changes during an animation
The lambda reads the state during layout, so a change only re-runs placement instead of recomposing the composable
The lambda form caches the offset once and reuses it, so the state is only read a single time in total
questions.explanation: Compose tracks state reads per phase: reading in a composable body invalidates composition, reading inside a layout or draw lambda only invalidates that phase. Moving per-frame reads into `offset { }`, `graphicsLayer { }` or `drawBehind { }` skips composition entirely for those frames. Everything still runs on the main thread (drawing then continues on RenderThread).

questions.question: Which statements about Compose's phases and state reads are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A state read inside `Modifier.drawBehind { }` only invalidates the draw phase when it changes
Reading state in an `onClick` lambda subscribes the composable to that state and recomposes it on change
A state read in a composable's body makes that recompose scope recompose when the state changes
A frame goes through composition, then layout (measure and place), then drawing
Layout runs before composition, so measuring a child can change which composables are emitted
questions.explanation: Composition decides what UI to emit, layout measures and places it, and draw renders it; each phase tracks the state it reads. Composition comes first (SubcomposeLayout is the explicit tool for composing during measurement). Event handlers run outside any phase, so state read there is not observed and causes no recomposition.

questions.question: LeakCanary reports an Activity leaked through a listener stored in a companion object. ART's GC handles reference cycles fine, so why is this still a leak?
options: ART uses reference counting, and the listener's reference cycle with the Activity can never be released
A static field is a GC root, so the listener and the Activity it captures stay reachable after onDestroy
The Activity is kept only until the next GC; LeakCanary flags it too early, before GC has a chance to run
Companion objects live in native memory, which ART's garbage collector does not scan for references
questions.explanation: Tracing GC frees whatever is unreachable from roots, cycles included; a leak means something still reachable holds the object. Static fields (companion objects, singletons) are roots for as long as the class is loaded, which here is the whole process lifetime. LeakCanary forces a GC before reporting, so a reported leak survived collection.

questions.question: When the system kills a backgrounded app's process, the ViewModel's in-memory state survives, because ViewModels are kept by the system across process death.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: ViewModels survive configuration changes because the ViewModelStore is retained across Activity recreation, but nothing in memory survives the process being killed. What comes back is saved state: `SavedStateHandle`, `rememberSaveable` and the navigation back stack. You can test this with 'Don't keep activities' for recreation or by killing the process from Android Studio for process death.

questions.question: With hardware acceleration, what does the main (UI) thread hand to RenderThread for each frame?
options: Recorded drawing commands (display lists on RenderNodes), which RenderThread turns into GPU work
Compressed textures for each view, which RenderThread uploads once and reuses on every frame
Measured sizes and positions only, from which RenderThread runs the views' onDraw methods
A finished bitmap of the whole window, which RenderThread copies to the display buffer
questions.explanation: On the UI thread, views (and Compose, through its own layers) record draw operations into display lists; RenderThread then issues the GPU commands, and can run some animations such as ripples without the main thread. This split is why a property change like translation or alpha on a layer can redraw without re-recording. A busy main thread still causes jank because recording happens there.

questions.question: Why is allocating new objects every frame (e.g. in onDraw or a per-frame draw lambda) still a problem when ART's GC runs mostly concurrently?
options: ART cannot allocate on the main thread at all, so each allocation is handed off to the GC thread instead
Each allocation is written to disk before use, so per-frame allocations add I/O cost to the frame
Concurrent GC is only used for large objects, so small per-frame allocations always cause a full pause
A high allocation rate makes GC run more often, using CPU on other cores and adding short pauses that can cost frames
questions.explanation: Concurrent collectors still have brief synchronisation pauses and use CPU time and memory bandwidth, which compete with the UI and RenderThread for a 16 ms (or 8 ms at 120 Hz) budget. More allocation means more frequent cycles. That is why Lint warns about allocations in onDraw and why per-frame paths reuse objects.

questions.question: Which statements about Compose stability inference are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A class from a module not compiled with the Compose compiler is treated as unstable unless listed in a stability config file
A data class with a `var` property is still inferred stable, as long as the property's type is String
A data class whose properties are all `val` with stable types (Int, String, other stable classes) is inferred stable
`ImmutableList` from kotlinx.collections.immutable is inferred unstable, just like `List`
`@Immutable` is a promise to the compiler that it does not check; breaking it can cause skipped updates
questions.explanation: The compiler can only infer stability for code it compiles, so other modules need the stability configuration file or wrapper types. A plain `var` property can change without Compose knowing, so the class is unstable. kotlinx immutable collections are treated as stable, which is why they are a common fix for `List` parameters.
